title: Total Solar Eclipse Sweeps Europe as Spain Witnesses First Mainland Blackout in Over a Century
excerpt: The first total solar eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999 crossed Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain on August 12, with the Perseid meteor shower peaking the same night.
body:
• A total solar eclipse swept across Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain on August 12 — the first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999.
  • Totality lasted up to 2 minutes and 18 seconds, with Spain experiencing the phenomenon near sunset as the eclipsed sun hovered just degrees above the western horizon.
  • Roughly 1 billion people globally fell under either the path of totality or a partial eclipse, spanning Europe, Canada, the northern U.S., and northwest Africa.
  • The Perseid meteor shower peaked the same night under new-moon darkness, creating a rare double celestial event.

A total solar eclipse raced across the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday, plunging parts of Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain into sudden darkness in what astronomers called one of the most dramatic celestial events in decades. For mainland Europe, it marked the first total solar eclipse since 1999 — and the first for mainland Spain since 1905.

The moon's shadow touched down near the North Pole before sweeping south across eastern Greenland, western Iceland, and the North Atlantic, then crossing into Spain's Galicia region in the northwest and tracking eastward toward the Balearic Islands. Maximum totality lasted 2 minutes and 18 seconds off Iceland's west coast, according to NASA.

"It feels like it's the end of the world ... you're changed forever if you see one."

— Elizabeth Warning, eclipse chaser, speaking to AFP

A Sunset Eclipse Like No Other

What made this eclipse unusual was its timing. In Spain, totality arrived in the early evening, with the sun sitting low on the western horizon. Observers in Valencia experienced totality at approximately 8:32 p.m. local time, with the sun hovering just four degrees above the horizon. In Galicia, the eclipsed sun stood at roughly 11 degrees — still remarkably low by eclipse standards.

https://x.com/FT/status/2087658592031690987

The geometric challenge turned location planning into the make-or-break decision for eclipse chasers. Cities like León, Burgos, and Palencia offered the most favorable conditions thanks to flat, open terrain with unobstructed western views. A ridge, building, or tree in the wrong place could block the entire spectacle, USA Today reported.

The path of totality stretched 190 miles (305 kilometers) wide as it crossed Spain, according to NASA data.

A Billion Eyes on the Sky

Beyond the narrow band of totality, a deep partial eclipse was visible across nearly all of Europe. London saw roughly 91% of the sun obscured. Dublin experienced 94% coverage. Cardiff hit 93%. Even Oslo, Norway, well north of the path, witnessed 83% of the solar disc disappear behind the moon.

In the United States, viewers in parts of the Northeast, Midwest, and Alaska caught a partial eclipse — a small bite out of the sun rather than the full show. The European Space Agency livestreamed the event from Spain's Astrophysical Observatory of Javalambre, while NASA provided coverage from multiple feeds.

Major European sporting events, including the UEFA Super Cup between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa, coincided with the eclipse's evening timing across the continent. Tournament organizers confirmed no schedule adjustments were made, with standard floodlight protocols handling any localized dimming effects.

Science Above and Below

The eclipse was far more than a spectacle. U.S. college research teams launched more than 60 high-altitude balloons from Spain and Iceland to study atmospheric changes during the brief window of darkness. Southwest Research Institute's Amir Caspi led a study aboard a NASA high-altitude jet, using four cameras to record the sun's corona in nine wavelengths while chasing the eclipse at 460 mph — extending totality to nearly three minutes in the air.

Two of ESA's space telescopes also observed the eclipsed sun. Proba-3, the agency's artificial eclipse-making satellite duo, was in the wrong part of its orbit during totality but attempted before-and-after observations.

"For me, it's not just a scientific moment. It's not just an incredible alignment of heavenly bodies. It's also a very human moment."

— Carole Mundell, Director of Science, ESA

Spain's Celestial Hat Trick

Wednesday's eclipse was the first of three solar eclipses Spain will host within a 532-day window. A second total eclipse on August 2, 2027, will track across southern Spain from Cádiz to Málaga and into North Africa, lasting up to 6 minutes and 23 seconds — one of the longest totalities visible from land in decades. An annular "ring of fire" eclipse will follow on January 26, 2028.

Adding to the spectacle, the Perseid meteor shower approached its annual peak just hours after the eclipse ended, with the new moon providing ideal dark-sky conditions. Six planets formed a pre-dawn arc earlier in the day, completing what astronomers described as an unprecedented day of celestial alignment.
